m00.body:
## What this pack is steering

The rep's brief is narrow and locked: **veterinary practices in Orkney** (GB), direct motion, email only, ten targets wanted, three weeks. Everything below is set before a single search, from the facts file and the knowledge set only.

### The spine

Insights360 is a post-call contact-centre intelligence product: it takes recordings the customer's own phone system already made, transcribes them, scores every ingested call against the customer's own QA rules, flags risk types the customer defines, and shows it all in a web app within a couple of hours. It does not record calls, does nothing during a live call, and has no agent login. The commercial spine is coverage plus price: the enterprise QA tools the knowledge set names sit at £36–£160 per seat per month with 50–400 seat minimums and multi-year commitments, while Insights360 is £4.99–£9.99 per seat per month with no seat minimum and no annual lock-in — against a one-off £1,280 setup fee and a £640 configuration review at about month one.

### What is being displaced

The incumbent is not a rival product. It is the practice's own ears: whoever happens to overhear the front desk, plus a complaint that arrives after the fact. In the knowledge set's own framing, manual QA reaches 2–5% of calls and the rest is invisible. In a veterinary practice the equivalent is that nobody reviews reception calls at all, and the first signal that a call went wrong is a client leaving, a review appearing, or a complaint reaching the practice principal.

### The tension this brief has to survive

Two product-level constraints sit directly across the brief, and the campaign agent must see them before it reads anything else. First, the knowledge set's explicit exclusion: sub-five-seat operations are not the ICP, because £4.99 a seat against a £1,280 setup fee does not work for either side. Second, the setup fee itself: there is no free or instant start, so a very small practice has to find over £1,900 of one-off cost before the per-seat price becomes the conversation. Orkney is a small archipelago. Whether ten veterinary practices of viable size exist there at all is the first thing this research must establish, and it is the question the scope decision turns on.

### What must not lead

The facts file's notes are binding wording. Several of the most attractive-sounding lines are barred outright: real-time anything, listening to a recording inside the app, regulator-ready evidence packs, per-team scorecards, a group view across several practices, SSO, PII redaction, a retention policy, and any promise that Insights360 catches literally every call a practice makes. The honest coverage claim is 'every call we ingest'. Hosting is EU (Frankfurt), not UK — the brand-voice article's 'never leaves UK Vercel + AWS' example is wrong and must not be repeated. Sentiment comes from Bedrock, not Comprehend, whatever the overview and integrations articles say.

### Hypotheses carried in

No prior packs exist for this product and org, so nothing is inherited. The knowledge set's ICP baseline offers three shapes worth testing against what Orkney actually contains: a priced-out small operation, a manual-QA floor manager whose sampling has stopped meaning anything, and a buyer locked into a platform whose QA module they cannot unbundle. All three assume a contact centre. A veterinary practice has a reception desk, not a contact centre, and that gap is the central risk in the brief.
m00.spine: Post-call scoring of every ingested recording from the phone system a practice already has, at £4.99–£9.99 per seat per month with no seat minimum and no annual lock-in, against a one-off £1,280 setup fee and a £640 configuration review at about month one.

m00.displacement: Displaces nobody reviewing reception calls at all: the practice's current quality signal is an overheard conversation, a client who quietly leaves, or a complaint that arrives after the damage. m01.body:
## The whole market, counted

Orkney's veterinary market is two businesses. Not two dozen, not ten — two. Orkney.com, the islands' official destination and business site, tells dog owners plainly that "Orkney has two veterinary practices, both of which offer an out of hours emergency service", and names them: Flett & Carmichael and Northvet. The Scottish Government's own Highlands and Islands Veterinary Services Scheme register, last updated 31 July 2026, lists three Orkney entries, but two of them are Northvet premises (Kirkwall and Harray) and the third is Flett & Carmichael. Two commercial directories put the Orkney number at four — that count is premises, not organisations: it splits Northvet's Kirkwall, Harray and Stromness surgeries into three rows and adds Flett & Carmichael.

So the campaign agent should read every "four practices in Orkney" figure it meets as four registered veterinary premises operated by two firms. That distinction decides the brief. Ten targets were asked for. Two organisations exist.

## What the two look like

The two are not the same shape, and the difference matters more than their number.

Northvet Veterinary Group Ltd is the larger by a wide margin. Its own listing describes seven veterinary surgeons, three veterinary nurses, an animal nursing assistant, a practice manager and eight reception and administration staff; its current recruitment describes a twelve-vet team; and when its director spoke to Orkney Islands Council's planning committee about a proposed new Kirkwall building she put the business at around 32 full- and part-time employees. It runs three premises, covers the outer isles, and provides 24-hour emergency cover 365 days a year. It is the only organisation in the scope with a reception function large enough to be recognisable as the thing Insights360 was built for — and even then, eight reception and administration staff sits at the very bottom of the product's stated 5–250 seat band, and the knowledge set's own exclusion list treats operations that small as marginal (an inference from the m00 steering note, not from any page read this run).

Flett & Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons is a single-premises independent practice at Hatston Industrial Estate, Kirkwall, trading from Hatston Veterinary Centre Limited, an active Scottish company. Its website publishes opening hours, a 24-hour emergency line, and small-animal, farm and equine services. No staff count is published anywhere I could read this run. Nothing suggests a contact-centre-shaped reception; a single-site island practice of this kind would ordinarily be one or two people answering the phone (inference, not sourced).

## The clock that is actually ticking

The live regulatory event in this sector is not local. On 24 March 2026 the Competition and Markets Authority published the final decision report of its market investigation into veterinary services for household pets, and the CMA's own announcement says the legally binding Orders and undertakings must be in place by 23 September 2026. The British Veterinary Association's summary adds that businesses will have until early 2027 to comply. The remedies bite on client communication: written estimates where treatment is likely to cost £500 or more including VAT, itemised bills, comprehensive published price lists, and written policies and processes. Almost all of that is a front-desk conversation before it is a document — which is the only genuinely strong reason a veterinary practice anywhere in GB might care about what is said on its phone lines in the next six months.

That clock applies to both Orkney practices, and to every other veterinary practice in Great Britain. It is a sector trigger, not an Orkney trigger. Nothing found this run makes Orkney more exposed to it than Aberdeen or Inverness; if anything the island practices sit inside a Scottish Government support scheme that the rest of GB has no equivalent of.

## What this means for the pack

The rest of this pack has to be built on two firms. Three kinds of buyer with two seed firms each cannot be assembled from two organisations without either inventing firms or reusing one under two headings, both of which are barred. The honest reading of the landscape is that the brief's geography is smaller than the smallest viable campaign, not that the sector is wrong. That judgement goes to the scope decision, not to me to fix.

bodies.name: Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons (RCVS)
bodies.role: Statutory regulator of veterinary surgeons and veterinary nurses; operates the Practice Standards Scheme and the Find a Vet practice register
bodies.relevance: The register is the authoritative source for which premises exist in Orkney and what they are accredited for. The RCVS is also giving undertakings to the CMA as part of the March 2026 remedies package, so it is the body that will police the new client-communication rules.

bodies.name: Competition and Markets Authority (CMA)
bodies.role: Competition regulator; ran the market investigation into veterinary services for household pets
bodies.relevance: Its final decision report of 24 March 2026 sets the only dated, sector-wide compliance clock in this market. Orders due in place by 23 September 2026, compliance into early 2027. The remedies land on written estimates, itemised bills and published price lists — all of them front-desk conversations first.

bodies.name: Veterinary Medicines Directorate (VMD)
bodies.role: Regulator of veterinary medicines; inspects veterinary practice premises
bodies.relevance: Requires every premises supplying veterinary medicines to be registered with the RCVS (£38 annually each April) and runs risk-based inspections. Relevant as a compliance surface a practice already carries, not as a call-quality driver.

bodies.name: Scottish Government — Highlands and Islands Veterinary Services Scheme (HIVSS)
bodies.role: Funding scheme ensuring adequate veterinary provision to crofters and similar in the crofting counties, including Orkney
bodies.relevance: Both Orkney firms are participating practices. The scheme is the reason island practices carry farm work that would otherwise be uneconomic, and it is administered from Saughton House, Edinburgh. It also marks the Orkney practices as SMEs under the UK Companies Act 2006 definition.

bodies.name: British Veterinary Association (BVA) and its Scottish Branch
bodies.role: Representative body for the veterinary profession; Scottish Branch represents members in Scotland and includes a HIVSS representative on its council
bodies.relevance: The BVA is the clearest published interpreter of what the CMA remedies mean for practices and when, and its Scottish Branch is where island-practice concerns are aired. A venue and a voice, not a buyer.

bodies.name: Orkney Islands Council — Animal Welfare section, Environmental Health and Trading Standards
bodies.role: Local authority enforcement of animal health and welfare legislation and animal-business licensing in Orkney
bodies.relevance: The local regulatory counterpart to the practices, and — as its planning committee's refusal of Northvet's new surgery shows — the body whose decisions shape the practices' operating constraints. Not a veterinary practice, so out of scope as a target.

bodies.name: XLVets
bodies.role: Membership community of independent veterinary practices; runs a shared vacancies board
bodies.relevance: Northvet advertises through it, which makes XLVets a route by which independent island practices see supplier and peer information. Useful as a discovery surface; it is not a regulator and carries no compliance weight.

Commercial veterinary directories list four veterinary premises in Orkney: Northvet's Junction Road (Kirkwall), Lammaquoy (Harray) and North End Road (Stromness) sites, plus Flett & Carmichael at Hatston Veterinary Centre Ltd, Kirkwall.

claims.text: Flett & Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons operates from a single Kirkwall address at Garrison Road, Hatston Industrial Estate, KW15 1GN, open Monday to Friday 8.45am–6pm and Saturday 9am–12 noon, with a 24-hour emergency service, covering small animal, farm and equine work.
Hatston Veterinary Centre Limited (company number SC340215), registered at Hatston Veterinary Centre, Garrison Road, Hatston Industrial Estate, Kirkwall, Orkney KW15 1GN, is an active company.

Northvet Veterinary Group Ltd's Kirkwall premises is accredited under the RCVS Practice Standards Scheme at Core Standards (Equine), Core Standards (Farm Animal) and Small Animal General Practice, and is an RCVS Approved Graduate Development Practice.
The RCVS states that 65% of UK practices have earned Practice Standards Scheme accreditation, and that accredited practices are assessed every four years with spot checks possible at any time.

Under the CMA's final remedies package, veterinary businesses must provide a written estimate of the cost of treatment where it is likely to be £500 or more including VAT, provide itemised bills, and have written policies and processes; the CMA narrowed 21 proposed recommendations to 14 remedies to be implemented through a CMA Order and undertakings from the RCVS.

The Highlands and Islands Veterinary Services Scheme is funded by the Scottish Government to ensure provision of an adequate veterinary service for animals kept for agricultural purposes belonging to crofters and others of like economic status, and covers the former counties including Orkney; it is open to small and medium enterprises as defined in the UK Companies Act 2006.

Anyone operating a veterinary practice premises from which to supply veterinary medicines must first register that premises with the RCVS; the registration fee is £38 payable on first application and annually each April, and the Veterinary Medicines Directorate conducts risk-based inspections.
There are around 1,500 businesses based in Orkney, with more than 90% employing fewer than 10 people.

triggers.text: The CMA concluded its market investigation into veterinary services for household pets with a final decision report published 24 March 2026; the next stage gives the CMA six months to put legally binding Orders on businesses in place and to accept undertakings from the RCVS, so these will be in place by 23 September 2026.

triggers.text: The RCVS publicly responded to the CMA's final report of Tuesday 24 March 2026, broadly welcoming many remedies and its own future role in monitoring compliance by veterinary businesses, while voicing concern over certain recommendations.

Orkney Islands Council's planning committee refused Northvet's application for a new veterinary surgery between Hatston Brae and Grainbank, west Kirkwall, after 39 objections; eight councillors voted against, two in favour and one abstained, despite a planning-department recommendation for approval. Northvet's director told the committee the firm had been looking for new premises for ten years and that its Junction Road surgery has only six parking spaces.

On 25 August 2026 the RCVS notified users that technical updates to its Find a Vet service mean some practice information will not be available in the short term.

marketSize: Two veterinary businesses operate in Orkney: Northvet Veterinary Group Ltd and Flett & Carmichael Veterinary Surgeons (trading from Hatston Veterinary Centre Limited). Source: orkney.com's own dog-friendly guidance, corroborated by the Scottish Government's HIVSS participating-practices list.

Four registered veterinary premises across those two businesses: Northvet at 33 Junction Road, Kirkwall (KW15 1AG), Lamaquoy/Lammaquoy, Harray (KW17 2LQ) and 1 North End Road, Stromness (KW16 3AG); Flett & Carmichael at Garrison Road, Hatston Industrial Estate, Kirkwall (KW15 1GN).

Largest employer of the two: Northvet, at around 32 full- and part-time employees in total, of which 8 are reception/administration staff by the firm's own listing — the only reception function in the scope that approaches the product's stated 5-seat floor.

Whole-scope addressable seat count is therefore in the region of 8–12 reception and administration seats across both firms combined (derived: Northvet's stated 8 reception/administration staff plus an unsourced allowance for Flett & Carmichael, whose staff count is not published — treat as an estimate, not a figure from any page).
Context for scale: Orkney has around 1,500 businesses in total, more than 90% of them employing fewer than ten people.

It has 24-hour emergency phone cover, outer-isles coverage and a practice manager, so a call-quality conversation is at least coherent. Against it: eight admin seats at £4.99–£9.99 a month against a £1,280 setup fee and a £640 configuration review is a hard commercial case, and nothing found this run shows what telephony it runs.

Every one of them is outside the rep's locked scope, which names Orkney only. Listed here so the campaign agent can see what a widening would reach, not as targets.

insufficient.reason:
Orkney contains two veterinary organisations, not ten. Orkney.com's own guidance says "Orkney has two veterinary practices"; the Scottish Government's HIVSS list shows the same two; directories' "four practices" figure counts Northvet's three premises separately. The floor is three kinds of buyer with two seed firms each inside the scope — six distinct firms. Two exist, and a firm may be one seed only.

Size compounds it. Northvet, the larger, publishes 8 reception/administration staff out of ~32 employees; Flett & Carmichael is single-site and publishes no staff count. The product is built for 5–250 contact-centre seats and the knowledge set excludes sub-5-seat operations outright, so at best one of the two clears the floor, and only just, against a £1,280 setup fee plus a £640 configuration review.

The sector is not wrong — the CMA's 23 September 2026 Orders deadline is a real GB-wide clock on veterinary client communication. The geography is smaller than the smallest viable campaign.

widenings.text: Keep veterinary practices, drop Orkney, and run the brief across Great Britain. The CMA's 23 September 2026 Orders on client communication apply to every GB veterinary business, and the corporate veterinary groups run central client-contact teams at the seat sizes the product is built for.

Keep Orkney and add the rest of the Scottish islands and Highlands. The Scottish Government's HIVSS list names practices in Shetland, Lewis and Harris, Uist, Skye, Islay, Mull and Tiree alongside the Orkney two — same 24/7 island obligation, same scheme, same CMA deadline, roughly ten organisations instead of two.

Stay in Orkney and drop the veterinary-only filter. Orkney has around 1,500 businesses and a council employing over a thousand people; the question becomes which Orkney employers run a multi-seat phone desk with recorded calls, rather than which vets do. Expect a short list either way.
